sections.title_en: The Prohibition of Making Sculptures for Decoration
sections.body_en:
In addition to the prohibition of making sculptures for the sake of avoda zara (idolatry) (above 3:3), the Torah forbade making, for decoration, sculptures that those who see them might mistakenly imagine to possess power and influence, and might wish to worship as gods or as intermediaries between man and God. As it is stated (Shemot 20:19-20): "And the Lord said to Moshe: Thus shall you say to the Children of Israel: You yourselves have seen that I have spoken with you from heaven. You shall not make with Me gods of silver, and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves" (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:10).

The prohibition of making sculptures for decoration applies to three kinds of sculptures that might call to mind higher powers: a) the human form, b) the form of angels, c) the heavenly bodies.

The human form, as the Sages expounded (Avoda Zara 43b): "'You shall not make with Me (iti)' – you shall not make Me (oti)," for God reveals Himself to the prophets in an image of human form, as it is stated (Yeḥezkel 1:26): "And upon the likeness of the throne was a likeness as the appearance of a man upon it above." And it is stated (Bereshit 1:27): "And God created man in His image, in the image of God He created him."

Angels and heavenly bodies, as the Sages expounded (Avoda Zara 43b): "'You shall not make with Me' – you shall not make the likeness of My servants who serve before Me on high." In the upper realm: "such as the ofanim, the serafim, the holy ḥayot and the ministering angels," that is, sculptures that people perceive as these figures. In the lower realm: "such as the sun and the moon, the stars and the constellations." Likewise, it is forbidden to make a sculpture resembling the faces of the ḥayot (living creatures) that carry the Merkava (the Divine Chariot), which are described in Yeḥezkel as an image of God's conduct of the world. As it is stated (Yeḥezkel 1:6-10): "And every one had four faces, and every one of them had four wings… As for the likeness of their faces, they had the face of a man, and the face of a lion… and the face of an ox… and the face of an eagle." That is to say, the prohibition is to make a single figure that has four faces: in front the face of a man, on the right the face of a lion, on the left the face of an ox, and behind the face of an eagle. It is likewise forbidden to make, in place of the face of the ox, the face of a keruv (cherub; the face of a child), for the prophet Yeḥezkel asked that in the vision of the Merkava the form of the ox be changed to a keruv, so as not to recall the sin of the Golden Calf (Ḥagiga 13b).

However, it is permitted to make the image of each of the faces on its own. For the prohibition of making sculptures for decoration applies to the three kinds of sculptures that might call to mind higher powers, and not to sculptures of animals such as lions, sculptures of birds such as an eagle, or sculptures of trees and flowers and all other things in nature (Avoda Zara 43b; Rashi; SA YD 141:4, 6; Shakh 20).1

notes_en.en:
In the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael (Shemot 20:20): "Rabbi Natan says: 'You shall not make Me' – so that you should not say: I will make a kind of likeness for Him and bow down to it." Sefer Ha-ikarim 3:18 explained that the concern is that people will think these forms can mediate between man and God; and so wrote Ibn Ezra, Sforno and Abarbanel. Similarly, the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:10) that the reason for the prohibition of making forms for decoration is "so that those who err should not err by them and imagine that they are for worship." Rav Herzog explained that the gentiles would mistakenly think that Israel too errs in idolatry (Psakim U-khtavim 4:44). Below, in halakha 8, it will be explained that some were stringent not to make sculptures of animals either; however, the halakha is as explained above, that only three kinds of sculptures are forbidden for decoration.
Constellations: According to the Baḥ and the Taz 141:13, one should not draw the form of one of the twelve constellations, such as a lion, a ram and an ox. The Taz added that those who draw the forms of the constellations in maḥzorim do not act properly. However, the Shakh 141:30 rejected their words, writing that just as with the faces of the Merkava the prohibition applies only to the four faces together, so too with the twelve constellations. End quote. And many wrote that the prohibition applies only when they are drawn as they appear in the firmament, that is, as a cluster of stars or dots forming the shape of the constellation; but there is no prohibition at all against drawing or sculpting the symbolic figures after which the star clusters were named (Meiri, Avoda Zara 42b, s.v. "din oseh"; Yad Ketana on the Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 2, 3:33; Igrot Moshe YD 2:55; Divrei Yatziv YD 38:16).

sections.body_en:
The poskim disagree as to whether the three kinds of sculptures that are forbidden to make even for decoration are also forbidden to make as a drawing. Some are stringent, holding that whatever is forbidden in sculpture is forbidden in drawing. And some of the stringent opinions hold that it is permitted to draw the human form, since we are used to seeing a person with volume, and a drawing of him is entirely different. However, we are used to seeing the forms of the sun, moon and stars in the sky without volume, like a drawing, and therefore it is forbidden to draw them too. On the other hand, according to most poskim a drawing differs in its essence from a sculpture, and therefore all three kinds of forbidden sculptures are permitted as drawings.

In practice, it is permitted to draw a human figure, since this is the opinion of the great majority of poskim (below, 4). Regarding the forms of the sun, moon and stars, although most poskim are lenient, since the stringent opinions are also many, it is proper to be stringent in accordance with their view (below, 6). And even the servants of the upper realm, such as the ofanim, serafim, holy ḥayot and ministering angels, one should not draw le-khatḥila (from the outset).2

notes_en.en:
There are three ways of setting forms on a wall: a) a protruding form, a relief (three-dimensional), whose law is like that of a sculpture. b) A sunken form, an engraving, about which there is a dispute whether its law is like that of a sculpture. c) A flat drawing, that is, without volume, which many permit.
We will begin with the law of an engraving, listing the views of the poskim from the stringent to the lenient, and afterwards add the view of those who are lenient regarding a drawing. a) Whatever is forbidden in sculpture is forbidden in engraving as well (Ra'avad, Ramban, Ran, Avoda Zara 43b; Taz 141:12). b) Whatever is forbidden in sculpture is forbidden in engraving, except for a human being, which is forbidden only in relief but permitted in engraving (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:10; Orḥot Ḥayim). c) Only the servants of the lower realm – sun, moon, stars and constellations – are forbidden in engraving, but a human being and the servants of the upper realm such as angels are permitted in engraving (Rabbeinu Tam, Ri and Riva in Tosafot, Avoda Zara 43b, s.v. "ve-ha Rabban Gamliel"; Semag, Rabbeinu Peretz, Rosh, Avoda Zara 3:5; SA 141:4; Shulḥan Gavoha 22). d) Everything is permitted in engraving (Rashba, Semak, Behag as cited by the Ramban, Maharam of Rothenburg 3:24, and as cited in Tosafot, Yoma 54a, s.v. "keruvim", Rabbeinu Simḥa, and the Tur according to the Darkhei Moshe 141:5).
Regarding a flat drawing, some say that its law is like that of an engraving (Ra'avad, Shakh in Nekudot Ha-kesef; Leḥem Rav 15; Parashat Ha-kesef), and some hold that those who are stringent about an engraving are lenient about a drawing (Maharam, Taz 141:12; the Mordekhai as cited in the Darkhei Moshe 141:5; Knesset Yeḥezkel OḤ 13; Beit Shlomo YD 1:198; Mishmeret Shalom YD 141:3. This is also the view of the Ritva, except that in his opinion, if the ink has thickness, the drawing is considered a relief, whereas most poskim hold that its law is that of a drawing).

sections.title_en: The Prohibition of Keeping Forms, and Decorating the Home
sections.body_en:
As we learned in halakha 1, the Torah forbade making three kinds of sculptures that people might worship, even when they are made for decoration. In addition, the Sages forbade keeping in the house a sculpture that people customarily worship, lest the one who keeps it be suspected of wishing to worship it. This prohibition applies to any sculpture that people customarily worship at that time, including sculptures that are not of the three kinds the Torah forbade making for decoration, such as a dragon, which people used to worship in the past. However, since the sculpture was made for decoration and not for idolatry, it is not forbidden to derive benefit from it, and it is permitted to melt it down or sell it to a non-Jew (Avoda Zara 43b; SA and Rema 141:4; Shakh 24).

When there is no concern at all that a Jew will be suspected of wishing to worship the sculpture, for example when there are no longer people who worship it, it is permitted to keep it in the house, even if it is one of the three kinds forbidden to make – the human form, angels and heavenly bodies. However, some say that it is preferable not to decorate the house with something that a Jew is forbidden to make.3

notes_en.en:
In Avoda Zara 43b we learned that, in addition to the Torah prohibition of making sculptures that call to mind higher powers, such as a human being, angels and heavenly bodies, the Sages forbade a person to keep in his possession a sculpture that people customarily worship, because of suspicion. According to the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim, the suspicion is that people will think the owner of the sculpture worships it (Behag, Rashi, Tosafot, Ramban, Rashba, Rosh, Ra'ah and many others). And some say that the suspicion is also that he may have transgressed the prohibition of making a sculpture (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona and Meiri). The halakha follows the overwhelming majority of poskim, who are not concerned about this suspicion; therefore it is permitted to keep in the house a sculpture that people do not customarily worship, and only when there is a concern that the one keeping the sculpture worships it is it forbidden to keep it in the house.
There are two views on this: a) Only sculptures that many people customarily worship are forbidden to keep in the house, as explained in the Mishna (Avoda Zara 42b): the form of a dragon, the sun and the moon. And so too in every generation according to what many people customarily worship (Behag, Rashba, Ritva). b) Some are stringent, holding that any respected sculpture regarding which there is some chance that its owner will be suspected of worshipping it is forbidden to keep in the house, including respected sculptures of animals (Ramban, Radbaz). Rabbeinu Yeruḥam holds that this stringency applies only to sculptures mentioned in the Talmud, such as the three kinds derived from "You shall not make," and likewise a dragon, but not to sculptures of animals. In practice, from the time people ceased worshipping these sculptures in the countries where Jews live, there is no prohibition against keeping such sculptures in the house. And so ruled the Aḥaronim, among them: Ḥokhmat Adam 85:6; Ha'amek She'ala 57:3; Naḥal Eshkol 50:27; Da'at Kohen 65; Divrei Yatziv 4:38. And some were concerned and stringent, forbidding the keeping of human sculptures even when it is clear that they are not worshipped; see Ḥatam Sofer 6:6. And see Shakh 141:17, who wrote that this view has no source. Above I gave a reason for the custom of those who are stringent: that it is preferable not to decorate the house with sculptures that are forbidden to make.
The topic of the ring is central in the Gemara and the Rishonim, but since it is not practical in our times, we will summarise it in a note: Avoda Zara 43b: "It was taught: A ring whose seal is protruding – it is forbidden to wear it, but permitted to seal with it; its seal is sunken – it is permitted to wear it, but forbidden to seal with it." In the past, idolaters used to emboss in relief the forms of their gods, such as the form of the sun or of a man, on their rings, so that they could kiss them at any time. Many also used rings with such forms for decoration, or for sealing in wax with which they sealed letters or packages to prevent forgery. In the period when many people used to worship these forms, the Sages ruled that it is forbidden to wear a ring bearing a protruding form that people customarily worship, so that the wearer would not be suspected of worshipping it (Rabbeinu Ḥananel, Rashi, Ra'avad, Rashba, Ra'ah). But there is no prohibition against keeping this ring in one's pocket or keeping it in the house, for in this manner the idol is not esteemed and honoured, and consequently there is no suspicion (Perisha YD 141:25). Nor is there any prohibition against sealing with it, for the form made in the wax will be sunken. And if the form on the ring is sunken, it is permitted to wear it on one's finger for decoration, since it bears no form in relief that people worship; but it is forbidden to seal with it, since the sealing will create in the wax a relief of a form that people customarily worship. On the other hand, according to Tosafot, the Rosh, the Ritva, SA 141:5 and Shakh 28, the prohibition of wearing a protruding seal also includes keeping it in the house. The Yad Peshuta (Avoda Zara 3:11) explained that one should not keep a form in the house for decoration because of suspicion, but if there is a real need for the ring, to seal with it, there is no longer any suspicion. And some explain that the concern about keeping it in the house applies only to respected objects meant for decoration, for then there is room to suspect that the forms are for the sake of idols; but there is no prohibition against keeping forms that are on lowly objects, that is, objects meant for a particular use, such as a seal, since it is clear that they are not worshipped (Ramban, Ra'ah, Maharit).

sections.title_en: An Incomplete Human Form, Drawing and Photography
sections.body_en:
The prohibition is to make a sculpture of a complete person, with his face and his whole body – whether it is a sculpture complete on all sides, or a relief of his front side with his face and his whole body. But it is permitted to make a sculpture of a person that has a noticeable deficiency, for example omitting part of the ear or the tip of the foot. Likewise, it is permitted to make a bust, that is, a sculpture of a person with his exact face and the upper half of his body. It is likewise permitted to make a relief of a profile, since in a profile only one eye, one hand and one foot are seen (Rosh; SA and Rema 141:7). Some are stringent about this, but the halakha follows the view of most poskim.4

As stated above (halakha 2), according to the overwhelming majority of poskim it is permitted to draw a human figure, because the prohibition of making a human form is modelled on his actual appearance, and since a person appears to our eyes with volume, the prohibition applies only where the form has volume, like a sculpture or a relief, and not to a drawing in which his figure is flat (Tosafot; Rosh; SA 141:4 [the Hebrew reads 144:4]).

When cameras began to be developed, there were rabbis who, out of concern for pride and for the prohibition of making a form according to some poskim, took care not to be photographed and not to have their picture printed. However, over the years photography became very widespread, and with that the concerns that had accompanied it at first fell away. For there is no concern of pride in something that everyone does as a matter of routine. The concern of the prohibition of making a form according to some poskim also fell away, since the prohibition is to make a human form for decoration and art, but there is no prohibition against photographing a particular person for documentation and remembrance. In addition, as the craft of photography became more refined, taking a photograph became an easy action that is hard to define as a deed at all.5

notes_en.en:
Many wrote that there is no prohibition against making a sculpture of a person that is not complete (a bust), among them: Rosh (Avoda Zara 3:5), Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, Rabbeinu Peretz, Hagahot Maimoniyot, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and the Tur. And so ruled SA 141:7, and the Rema wrote that this is the practice. And so wrote Beit David, Yad Ha-ketana, Beit Hillel, Eliyahu Rabba, Nahar Shalom and others. However, the Semag (Lavin 22) forbade it. And so wrote the Maharit (YD 35) and the Ya'avetz (1:170). And Ḥokhmat Adam (85:4) and Ben Ish Ḥai (Year 2, Masei 10) were concerned for their view, since it is a doubt regarding a Torah law. And see Da'at Kohen 65. However, the halakha follows the view of most poskim, who permitted it.
Accordingly, it is permitted to make a complete sculpture if it is damaged. The question is how large the defect must be. According to the Ḥatam Sofer YD 128, a small defect suffices, such as damaging the top of its ear or the tip of its nose. According to the Beit Leḥem Yehuda YD 141, the entire nose must be removed, so that the deficiency will be noticeable. In practice, it seems that what is needed is a deficiency that an onlooker will notice at first glance, and this can also be in part of its ear. The Ḥatam Sofer wrote there further that a Jew who wishes to learn to be a sculptor for gentiles may, in time of need, make decorative sculptures without finishing them, for example making them without an eye, and his non-Jewish assistant will finish them for him.

As we learned in note 2, according to three of the four views, it is permitted to make an engraving of a person. Only according to the view of the Ra'avad, Ramban and Ran is it forbidden to make an engraving. And there is a dispute whether according to this view they would also forbid a drawing: according to the Ra'avad and the Shakh in Nekudot Ha-kesef, they would forbid a drawing as well; according to the Taz, Knesset Yeḥezkel, Beit Shlomo and others, a drawing is permitted. It emerges, then, that according to the overwhelming majority of Rishonim and Aḥaronim it is permitted to draw and to photograph a person. Nevertheless, when people began to be photographed, there were rabbis who were accustomed to forbid it or to be concerned for the prohibition, such as the Ḥakham Tzvi, who took care not to have his portrait drawn (She'elat Ya'avetz 1:170). And so wrote Divrei Malkiel 3:58 and Yaskil Avdi vol. 2, Kuntres Aḥaron YD 11, to be stringent. Ben Ish Ḥai (Year 2, Masei 9) wrote that by the letter of the law it is permitted, and that refraining is a custom of piety. Da'at Kohen 66 wrote that there are pious people who refrain from this, and their words have some basis, but the main view is that it is permitted. End quote. As photography became more common, even those who were scrupulous not to take photographs or be photographed themselves did not protest against someone who wished to photograph them, for one should not protest against someone who acts according to the halakha. Moreover, the clearer it became that the purpose of photography is documentation and not making a human form, the more the concern disappeared. And one can say that just as it is permitted to make forms of the sun for the purpose of study (below, halakha 7), so it is permitted le-khatḥila to photograph a person for documentation. Responsa Hillel Omer YD 63 wrote that there is even a virtue in this, that children will see their parents, remember them, and be strengthened in Torah and mitzvot.

sections.body_en:
Included in the prohibition that the Torah imposed on Israel of making a human sculpture for decoration, it is forbidden for a Jew to produce, by hand or by machine, small figurines of people in the form of soldiers, clowns, famous leaders of the past or dancing Ḥasidim. It is likewise forbidden to produce a relief of their front side. And although it is clear that these figurines are not intended for idolatry, we have already learned that the Torah forbade making human sculptures for decoration. But if non-Jews made them, since today nobody worships them, and there is no concern that the one keeping them will be suspected of wishing to worship them, there is no prohibition against keeping them in the house (Rashba; Rosh; Ritva; Ḥokhmat Adam 85:6). And as we learned (halakha 2 [it seems this should be halakha 3]), some are scrupulous not to decorate the house with figurines that a Jew is forbidden to make.

Clothing store owners are permitted to place life-size mannequins in their display windows and dress them in the clothes sold in the store. When the mannequins are incomplete, for example without ears, a Jew too is permitted to make them, but when they are complete, a Jew is forbidden to make them. And according to many, it is also forbidden for a Jew to ask a non-Jew to make complete mannequins for him. But if a non-Jew manufactures complete mannequins for the stores of non-Jews, a Jew is permitted to buy them for his store.6

notes_en.en:
As we learned in note 3, although the great majority of poskim hold that it is permitted to keep them, I gave a reason for the custom of those who are scrupulous in this matter: that they do not wish to decorate the house with figurines that a Jew is forbidden to make. But in time of need, such as for store owners, they need not refrain from using mannequins, all the more so when they have a deficiency, for then according to most poskim a Jew is permitted to make them.
The wax museum: A Jew is forbidden to create the figures in a wax museum, but it is permitted to buy them from a gentile. And if a Jew made the figures, some say that it is forbidden to visit the museum, so as not to support transgressors and benefit from their deeds (Avnei Yashfeh 1:151). And some say that it is permitted to visit, since there is no prohibition against keeping the figures (Aseh Lekha Rav vol. 5, Ketzarot 72). In practice, today non-Jews abroad make the figures, but according to most Rishonim it is forbidden for a Jew to ask them to make particular figures for him, because according to most Rishonim the prohibition of shevut applies to all Torah prohibitions, as it does on Shabbat. That is to say, a Jew is forbidden to ask a non-Jew to do something that is forbidden to a Jew by Torah law (see Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it 5, n. 9). But if the Jew transgressed and asked this of a gentile, it is permitted to benefit from what he made, since there are Rishonim who hold that there is no prohibition of shevut with regard to other prohibitions, and it follows that there is no prohibition in his actions. In addition, one authority raised the reasoning that if part of the sculpture is covered, for example its feet are in shoes, it is not considered complete (Responsa Or Yitzḥak vol. 1, YD 25). And although one should not permit a Jew to make such figures on the basis of his opinion, his reasoning may be added in order to benefit from figures that non-Jews made at the request of a Jew.

sections.title_en: Sculpting and Drawing the Sun, Moon, Stars and Constellations
sections.body_en:
The prohibition of making sculptures of the sun, moon, stars and constellations applies on condition that they are made complete, but it is permitted to make them incomplete. A moon at the beginning of the month (a crescent shape) is not considered incomplete, for this is its natural shape at the beginning or end of the month.7

As explained above (halakha 2), the poskim disagree regarding drawing. Some are lenient, because in their opinion the prohibition applies only to sculptures or reliefs, and perhaps also to engravings. And some are stringent, since the prohibition follows the way the heavenly bodies appear to our eyes, and to our eyes they appear like a drawing and not like a sculpture (above, note 2). And it is proper in practice to act in accordance with the stringent opinion.

However, as we learned, even according to the stringent opinion it is permitted to draw heavenly bodies when they are incomplete or partly hidden, such as the sun at sunset when part of it is beyond the horizon, or when a tree or flying birds hide part of it. Likewise, according to many of the stringent opinions, it is permitted to draw the sun or moon somewhat differently from their form – either when the artist does not know how to be precise, or when the painter wishes to draw them with artistic freedom, for example not being particular about their colour or about the rays coming out of the sun. Therefore it is permitted to let young children draw the sun and moon for their enjoyment, for presumably they will not be precise in their drawing. All the more so it is permitted to draw a smiling sun or a rising sun as a figure encouraging one to get up. Likewise, it is permitted to draw them for the purpose of study (as explained in the next halakha). Artists who are learning to draw and need to draw the sun, moon or stars may, in time of need, rely on the lenient opinion (as explained in the note).8

It is permitted to buy drawings or photographs of the sun, moon and stars and hang them in the house for decoration. It is true that some are accustomed to be stringent about this, for since according to many poskim it is forbidden to draw them, in their opinion it is not fitting to decorate the house and clothing with them (Shakh 141:27). However, the main halakhic view is that there is no prohibition in this, for even regarding sculptures of the sun and moon, which according to all opinions a Jew is forbidden to make, the Sages forbade keeping them only when there is a concern that the person who keeps them will be suspected of intending to worship them secretly. But today, when it is not common for people to worship them, there is no prohibition (Ḥokhmat Adam 85:6; above, halakha 3). All the more so there is no prohibition against buying and keeping landscape paintings with heavenly bodies, which according to many poskim a Jew is permitted to draw. Likewise, it is permitted to buy blankets and clothes that bear these forms, and it is likewise permitted to give children prizes in the shape of stars to stick in their notebooks.

notes_en.en: As we learned in note 4, it is permitted to make a sculpture of a person that is not complete, and many wrote that it is also permitted to make the heavenly bodies incomplete. So wrote Responsa Maharam Alshikh 77 regarding the sun and moon. And so wrote Rav Pe'alim vol. 4, YD 10, except that he required placing them in a place where many people are present, to prevent suspicion. And some are stringent not to make an incomplete moon, since by its nature it is sometimes incomplete (Shevet Ha-levi 7:134:7; Ḥut Shani, Pesaḥ, p. 236), and so it is implied from Responsa Maharit (YD 35) and Sho'el U-meshiv (Mahadura Kamma vol. 3, 71). It seems that their intention is a moon in its natural shape at the beginning or end of the month, but if it is incomplete in a way that differs from its nature, it is permitted.

See above, note 2, that Rishonim and Aḥaronim disagree whether the prohibition of making the forms of the heavenly bodies includes a prohibition of drawing or not. And it seems that the same law applies to assembling a jigsaw puzzle. In practice many are accustomed to be lenient about drawing, and the poskim wrote further reasons for their custom: Some say that the prohibition is to draw them precisely, so that it "is recognisable to all as the appearance of the sun, that is, that there be prominent rays around the circle like the rays of the sun when it rises" (Mahari'atz vol. 2, YD 83:2; and similarly Rav Ḥayim Kassar in Shem Tov on the Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:11; Rav Orenstein in the name of the Maharil Diskin, cited in Tzitz Eliezer 9:44:8). And some say that the prohibition applies only when one draws the heavenly bodies on a sky-blue background, like their appearance in the sky (Meiri, Avoda Zara 42b, in the name of "some say"). The forbidden form of a star is round, as it appears in the sky, and not five-pointed as a symbol for a star, as in the flag of the United States.
And there is a more lenient opinion, according to which the entire prohibition of making the three kinds of sculptures applies only in the context of idol worship, in such a way that one who sees their form knows that they were made for this purpose, or that similar ones are customarily worshipped; but there is no prohibition against making the sun, moon and stars where they cannot possibly have an idolatrous meaning (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishna, Avoda Zara 3:3; and see Rav Kafiḥ on Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:10). And some combined this opinion to be lenient regarding drawing (Da'at Kohen YD 64; Beit Avi 2:75; and others. However, the Shakh 141:8 explained that according to this reasoning the Rambam permitted only deriving benefit from the value [?] of vessels that were found).
Regarding photographing the heavenly bodies, although the photograph is precise, there is room to be more lenient than with drawing, for the photograph is merely a copy made by means of electrical signals and their projection on a screen, and this is not similar to drawing on paper (and see Aseh Lekha Rav 6:54; Ohel Ya'akov 141, n. 30).

sections.title_en: For the Purpose of Study and Play
sections.body_en:
The prohibition of making sculptures of a person, angels and heavenly bodies applies to making them for decoration, but it is permitted to make them for a particular need, such as for study (Avoda Zara 43b; SA 141:4). Accordingly, it is permitted to make a doll in the form of a person in order to teach about the human body (anatomy). It is likewise permitted to make forms of the sun, moon and stars in order to teach through them the courses of the heavenly bodies (astronomy). All the more so it is permitted to print in a book pictures of the sun, moon and stars in order to learn about their course in the sky, for we have already learned (in halakha 5 [it seems this should be halakha 6]) that some say that even not for study it is permitted to draw the sun, moon and stars, since the prohibition is only to make sculptures in their form.9

It is permitted to manufacture dolls in human form for children's play, since the dolls are not manufactured for decoration and honour in a way somewhat similar to idolatrous sculptures, but for children's play in a way that involves no honour. The proof is that sometimes the doll is put on the ground and gets dirty (Maharit). All the more so it is permitted to buy dolls and play with them. It is true that some are stringent not to keep a complete doll in the house without damaging something in its face, but the halakha does not follow them, since these dolls are not treated with honour in a way that might recall idolatry. It is permitted to make snowmen, and human figures from plasticine, for they are made as a kind of play for a short time and not for decoration and honour.10

notes_en.en: In Avoda Zara 43b it is explained that although it is forbidden to make forms of the moon, Rabban Gamliel made them for the purpose of sanctifying the new month, because "for the purpose of learning it is different, as it was taught: 'You shall not learn to do' – but you may learn in order to understand and to teach." And we learned likewise regarding sorcery (Sanhedrin 68b; below 19:3). Some say that it is permitted to make forbidden forms only for the purpose of studying halakha, but for the purpose of learning an art it is forbidden (Ḥatam Sofer YD 128), and it is likewise forbidden for the purpose of studying anatomy (Rav Goren in Torat Ha-refu'a). However, in practice many permitted making forms of the sun and moon for the purpose of studying astronomy (Ria'z, Avoda Zara, Piskei Ha-ria'z 3:11; Meiri 43a; Shakh in Nekudot Ha-kesef 141:2; Rav Tchorsh). And some are even more lenient, holding that whenever it is clear that the form is not for idolatry there is no prohibition (Maharit YD 35; Mahari Mintz, Derashot 7; Aseh Lekha Rav 6:54).

Maharit YD 35 permitted making dolls for play, for the whole reason the Torah forbade making forms is in order to set them up in an honoured and permanent manner, for then there is a concern that people will mistakenly worship them; but for play, since it is clear that they are not for honour, there is no concern that people will mistakenly worship them. And so wrote the Responsa of Rav Kafiḥ 37; Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:64. All the more so it is permitted to buy dolls that have already been made and play with them, as we learned (note 3) that according to the overwhelming majority of poskim, the prohibition the Sages imposed against keeping sculptures and forms applies only where one might be suspected of worshipping them, but where there is no concern it is permitted. It is true that some were stringent to consider a doll a sculpture that is forbidden to keep without damaging something in its face (Shevet Ha-levi 7:134; and Ḥut Shani, p. 232, was concerned for this view le-khatḥila). However, since the basis of the prohibition of keeping is rabbinic, and in addition the overwhelming majority of poskim were lenient, it is permitted le-khatḥila to buy dolls and play with them. It is even permitted to manufacture dolls, and although a few of the Aḥaronim of our time are concerned that this involves a Torah prohibition, since most poskim hold that making a doll for play has no connection whatsoever to the prohibition of making a sculpture for decoration, one may rely on them and be lenient; and consequently one may also reattach the doll's arm if it has fallen off, and anything similar.

sections.title_en: Sculptures and Pictures of Animals in a Synagogue
sections.body_en:
As we learned (halakha 1), it is permitted to make sculptures of wild animals such as a lion, an elephant and a deer; of domestic animals such as an ox; of birds such as a dove and an eagle; and likewise of fish, trees, plants and everything in nature (SA 141:6).

In the days of the Rishonim, it was customary in Ashkenaz to adorn synagogues with sculptures or pictures of animals, birds and snakes, in order to express the song of the animals and birds to God, and also to beautify and glorify the synagogue. Above all they used to make forms of lions, thereby expressing the kingship of God – that even the lion, the king of the beasts, gives honour to his Creator, the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. This is like the "keruvim, the work of a skilled weaver" that were woven on the curtains of the Mishkan, which had the face of a lion on one side (Shemot 26:1 and Rashi; Maḥaneh Ḥayim YD 2:29). There is also in this an allusion to the words of the Mishna, "Be… mighty as a lion to do the will of your Father in heaven" (Avot 5:20; Heikhal Yitzḥak OḤ 11). Some used to place sculptures of lions at the sides of the Holy Ark or above it, with the form of the Tablets of the Covenant between them in honour of the Torah, and some used to embroider forms of lions on the parokhet (Ark curtain).

On the other hand, many criticised their custom: although according to virtually all poskim there is no prohibition against making a sculpture of an animal or bird, in their opinion in a synagogue one should be stringent in accordance with the individual opinions that forbid it, especially regarding the form of a lion, which is the form of the constellation of the month of Av and the form of one of the ḥayot of the Merkava. Moreover, if the sculptures or pictures of the lions stand facing the worshippers, the worshippers appear to be bowing down to them. Moreover, the sculptures or pictures may impair concentration and distract the worshippers. In Islamic lands there was an additional problem, for under the inspiration of Judaism the Muslims fought zealously against all kinds of sculptures, and there was a concern that if Jews set up sculptures of animals in a synagogue, the Muslims would scorn them for not being careful about idolatry, and might even come to smash the lions and damage the synagogue on the pretext that they had come to eradicate idolatry.

In practice, following the ruling of the great rabbis of Sepharad, already more than four hundred years ago the custom of setting up sculptures of lions in the synagogues of those of Sephardic descent was abolished. Many of those of Sephardic descent refrain even from reliefs and embroidery of lion forms on the parokhet.

In Ashkenaz too the custom of setting up sculptures of lions greatly diminished; however, with the consent of the great rabbis they used to adorn the Holy Ark with reliefs of lions of which only one side is visible (a profile), and often placed the form of the Tablets of the Covenant between the lions. They likewise used to adorn the parokhet with embroidery of lions. They explained that when the form of the lions is from the side, it is incomplete, and then even the few Rishonim who were stringent about a complete sculpture would agree that there is no prohibition. Nor is there a concern that onlookers will think the congregation worships them, for nobody is accustomed to bow down to a picture of lions. Nor is there a concern that these forms will distract the worshippers, since they were set up for the honour of Heaven and the congregation is used to them.11

notes_en.en:
Some forbid making sculptures of any animal or bird but permit drawing them (Tosafot, Yoma 54a-b, s.v. "keruvim"; Maharam of Rothenburg). Their source is the Mekhilta (Shemot 20:4), which learned this from the verses (Devarim 4:16-18): "Lest you deal corruptly and make for yourselves a graven image, the form of any figure… the likeness of any beast… the likeness of any winged bird… the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground." And some forbid even drawing them (Rabbeinu Elyakim, father-in-law of the Ra'avan, cited by Maharaḥ Or Zaru'a in Hagahot Asheri, Avoda Zara 3:5). However, the view of the other Rishonim and Aḥaronim is that the prohibition is to make them in order to worship them, but not in order to worship them it is permitted. So wrote the Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:11; Ran; SA YD 141:6; Perisha 20; Bi'ur Ha-Gra 31; and others. And some opposed making a sculpture of a lion, because it is one of the faces of the Merkava and also one of the constellations, but permitted it in a drawing (Baḥ, Taz 141:13). However, the Shakh 30 wrote that we have not heard of anyone who forbade this, for the prohibition of making the constellations or the faces of the Merkava applies only when one makes all of them together, as emerges from Tosafot, Avoda Zara 33a [perhaps 43a], s.v. "lo ta'asun." And so it is proven from all the Rishonim, among them Rashba 1:167, who ruled in accordance with the words of Abaye in Avoda Zara 43b, that the prohibition of the four ḥayot of the Merkava applies specifically when all of them are together.
On this basis, already about nine hundred years ago it was customary in Ashkenaz to adorn the synagogue with sculptures of animals such as lions and snakes, or with pictures of them. It is true that Rabbeinu Elyakim ruled that they be removed from the synagogue in Colonia (today Cologne), because the earlier generations had not been accustomed to do so, for it involves a Torah prohibition; and moreover, the worshippers who bow toward the wall on which the forms were set appear to be bowing to them. However, Rabbeinu Efrayim of Regensburg responded to his arguments and upheld the custom, as many of the Rishonim of Ashkenaz mentioned (Ra'avya, Elef 49; Agudah, Avoda Zara 3:38; Maharam of Rothenburg 4:610; Mordekhai, Avoda Zara 840).
Nearly five hundred years ago, Rabbi Eliyahu Capsali of Candia, the capital of the island of Crete, sent a question to the great rabbis of Sephardic descent, whether to accept a donation of a lion sculpture for the synagogue. The rabbis ruled to forbid it, in accordance with the view of some of the Rishonim who were stringent about this, with the addition of further reasons, as cited below (Responsa Radbaz 4:107; Avkat Rokhel 63; Maharam of Padua, there 65; Responsa Mabit 1:9). Rabbi Yosef Karo (Avkat Rokhel, there) added that even according to those who hold that in general one need not be concerned about suspicion that these sculptures are worshipped, in a synagogue there is more room for this concern. And regarding the form of a lion there is an additional stringency, since it is one of the forms that were in the Merkava that Yeḥezkel saw (1:10; above, halakha 1), and there is a greater concern that people will mistakenly worship it. And the Radbaz (4:107) added that since the lion is the king of the beasts, there is a greater concern that people will suspect that it is worshipped. It is worth noting that, except for the Maharam of Padua, who lived in Italy, the questioner and those asked lived in lands ruled by the Ottoman Muslims, who regarded every sculpture of an animal as outright idolatry that must be smashed.
Regarding embroidery of lions on the parokhet, the poskim in Islamic lands disagreed. Some were lenient on the basis of Rabbi Yosef Karo in Avkat Rokhel 66, who testified that this was the custom. And so ruled Responsa Simḥat Kohen OḤ 44, from Djerba, and Aseh Lekha Rav 1:40. On the other hand, some forbade it, and in their opinion Rabbi Yosef Karo too retracted in siman 63 from his responsum in siman 66, and his conclusion was to be stringent even regarding embroidery on the parokhet (Kerakh Shel Romi 4; Rav Uziel, as cited in Tzitz Eliezer 3:24; Yaskil Avdi 1, YD 5). And so ruled Shemo Yosef 214, from Algeria; Nehar Mitzrayim 1, YD Avoda Zara 7-8; Mayim Ḥayim OḤ 80, Morocco; Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:62. And some say that Rabbi Yosef Karo was lenient about embroidery only be-di'avad (after the fact) (Ḥesed Le-Avraham, Tinyana YD 39), but in practice it is proper to be concerned for the stringent opinion (Rabbi Shmuel Arkevolti, Asufot 7, pp. 96-99; Ikarei Ha-dat 19:11; Va-yomer Yitzḥak 1, OḤ 10, from Morocco; Yaskil Avdi 1, YD 5; and others). Many of the poskim of Islamic lands explained the stringency by the fact that the Muslims viewed this as idolatry (Rabbi Shmuel Arkevolti, there; Kuntres Taharat Ha-kodesh, cited by Yishrei Lev OḤ 90 and Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:62; Heikhal Yitzḥak OḤ 11; and similarly wrote the Radbaz 4:107).
In Ashkenaz, by contrast, although following the rulings of the rabbis of Sepharad (from the beginning of the period of the Aḥaronim) the custom of setting up lion sculptures gradually diminished, it continued to exist to some extent in the period of the Aḥaronim as well (see Neta Sorek YD 46; Meshiv Devarim YD 105). However, the custom of adorning the Holy Ark with reliefs of lions, or embroidering their form on the parokhet, continued to be widespread throughout Ashkenaz, as emerges from the testimony of many poskim (Darkhei Teshuva 141:48; Ma'arkhei Lev OḤ 9; Ḥesed Le-Avraham [Teomim] Tinyana YD 39; Igrot Ha-Re'iya 1:10; Heikhal Yitzḥak OḤ 11; Netzer Mata'ai 17; Divrei Yatziv YD 38; Igrot Moshe YD 2:55), and even in our days this is found in many synagogues. Many explained that the permission here is because the form of a lion in profile is considered incomplete (Maḥaneh Ḥayim YD 2:29; Divrei Yatziv YD 38; Heikhal Yitzḥak OḤ 11; Aseh Lekha Rav 1:40; Igrot Moshe YD 2:55; and others. This is unlike Darkhei Teshuva 141:48, who was stringent, or Ḥokhmat Adam 85:7 and several other poskim, who wrote that it is proper to be stringent. And some were stringent mainly in the Land of Israel; see Taharat Ha-kodesh and Ḥesed Le-Avraham).

sections.title_en: The Tablets of the Covenant on the Holy Ark
sections.body_en: For many generations it has been the custom of Israel in many synagogues throughout the world to adorn the Holy Ark or the parokhet with the form of the two Tablets of the Covenant, with their upper side rounded. In the previous generation some argued that this custom was learned from the gentiles, for according to the Talmud the Tablets were rectangular and not rounded at the top. However, halakhically one should not cast aspersions on all those who have followed this practice for many generations, for there is no need to make the Tablets as they were, neither in shape nor in size. On the contrary, we find that those who make vessels resembling the vessels of the Temple must make them differ from what was in the Temple.12

notes_en.en: As is well known, in thousands of synagogues throughout the world it has been customary to draw and sculpt the image of the Tablets of the Covenant with their upper part rounded, and in a few places they made them rectangular. In the previous generation, Rav Eliyahu Katz (Dibrot Eliyahu OḤ 1:96, from 5723) and the Lubavitcher Rebbe (in a talk in 5741) came out against the custom. However, in practice thousands of synagogues did not change the prevalent custom, and so wrote Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu in practice (Responsa of the Chief Rabbi 5748-5749, siman 198). And so they wrote in the name of Rav Elyashiv (Yisa Yosef OḤ 3:36). Mishneh Halakhot 15:169 even wrote that there is a virtue in their being round at the top, in order to differ from what was in the Temple. And so wrote Responsa Even Yisrael 8:57, though he also questioned whether in the Temple they were square. And some learned from the Zohar (vol. 2, 84b) that the upper side was round, for they were formed from two drops of dew, as Rav Avraham Azulai, author of Ḥesed Le-Avraham, wrote in his commentary on the Zohar, Or Ha-ḥama, that the Tablets were partly round and partly square.

sections.title_en: The Prohibition of Making a Building and Vessels Like Those of the Temple
sections.body_en:
Because of the honour of the Temple and the reverence due to it, the Torah forbade building a house in the form of the Temple or making vessels in the form of the Temple vessels, as it is stated (Shemot 20:20): "You shall not make with Me" – you shall not make the likeness of the Temple and its vessels, which are designated for the service of God. Accordingly, a person should not build a house with the length, width and height of the Temple. Nor should he make an akhsadra, that is, a structure open to the air, with the dimensions of the Ulam (Hall) that stood in front of the Sanctuary. Nor should he make a courtyard with the dimensions of the courtyard of the Azara (Temple Courtyard). Nor should he make a table or a menora in their form in the Temple (Avoda Zara 43a; Ḥinukh 254; SA 141:8).

But if he changes them somewhat, it is permitted, for the dimensions of the Temple and its vessels are exact, as it is stated (I Divrei Ha-yamim 28:19): "All this in writing, by the hand of the Lord upon me, He gave me understanding of all the works of the pattern," and anything that has been changed somewhat is not fit for the Temple, and consequently a Jew is permitted to make it (Rashi; Tosafot, Yoma 54b; Shakh 33). Likewise, it is permitted to build reduced-scale models of them, since they are unfit for the Temple. In practice, architects and vessel manufacturers need not study the size of the Temple and its vessels in order to take care not to make anything like them. For the chance that they will happen to make a house or an akhsadra exactly with the length, width and height of the Temple is negligible. Likewise, the chance that they will make a courtyard or a table of the size of what was in the Temple is very low. Accordingly, the prohibition is for a person to study the measurements of the Temple or the form of its vessels and build something like them. Even when non-Jews have built a structure or vessel in this manner, a Jew is forbidden to use them, because using them outside the framework of the Temple service involves an affront to the honour of Heaven (Rashba, Ra'ah and Ritva).13

Any menora made of ordinary metal that has seven branches is fit, in time of pressing need, for fulfilling with it the mitzva of lighting the lamps of the Menora, as was done in the days of the Ḥashmona'im when they were still poor and had no possibility of making the Menora of gold with all the ornaments described in the Torah (Avoda Zara 43a). Accordingly, it is forbidden to make a metal menora with seven branches, and if one made one, he must remove one branch or add one branch, but he should not leave it with its seven branches. It is permitted to make a seven-branched menora of another material that is not metal, such as wood or plastic (SA 141:8). It is likewise permitted to make a metal menora with seven branches and electric bulbs, since this menora is completely different from the Menora in the Temple.14

notes_en.en:
In the Gemara, Avoda Zara 43a, the prohibition of making the pattern of the Temple and its vessels is learned from the verse "You shall not make with Me," which is also the source for the prohibition of making sculptures and heavenly bodies, and this implies that the prohibition is from the Torah. And so it emerges from the words of the She'iltot (Yitro 57), Tosafot (Avoda Zara 43b, s.v. "lo"), the Meiri (Avoda Zara 43a) and the Maharik (siman 75). And so wrote Minḥat Ḥinukh 254:9; Bekhor Shor, Rosh Ha-shana 24a; Mitzvat Re'iya 670:1. (The Rambam, Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 7:10, did not cite this prohibition in Hilkhot Avoda Zara but rather as part of the laws of reverence for the Temple, and so did the Ḥinukh 254. Some learned from this that in their opinion the prohibition is rabbinic – Kiryat Sefer of the Mabit; Beit Efrayim OḤ 10; Ḥatam Sofer, Avoda Zara 43a. And according to the Minḥat Ḥinukh 254:8-11, according to the Rambam too the prohibition is from the Torah.)
There are four sizes of the Temple: the Mishkan, as explained in the Torah, Shemot 26; the First Temple, as explained in I Melakhim, chapter 6; the Second Temple, as explained in tractate Middot; and the Third Temple, as explained in the book of Yeḥezkel, chapters 40-44. According to many, the prohibition is to make a structure like any one of the four sizes (Beit Efrayim OḤ 10, cited in Pitḥei Teshuva 141:13; Igrot Moshe YD 3:33). On the other hand, the Minḥat Ḥinukh (254:9) inclined to say that the prohibition follows the Temple that is standing at that time, and consequently today, when the Temple is destroyed, there is no prohibition; but in practice he was wary of being lenient regarding a Torah prohibition.
There is no prohibition against building a structure resembling the chambers, the Ezrat Nashim (Women's Courtyard) or the courtyard on the Temple Mount, since they are not indispensable to the existence of the Temple and its service (Mikdash David, Beit Ha-beḥira 1:3). The Minḥat Ḥinukh 254:13 wrote that it stands to reason that the prohibition includes all the vessels whose form is explicit in the Torah, such as the Table and the Altar; but vessels that are not specified in the Torah are permitted.
It is forbidden to keep vessels that non-Jews made. So wrote the Nimukei Yosef in the name of the Rashba; and the Ra'ah, Ritva and Meiri on Avoda Zara 43a. It is true that some were lenient to keep them, just as it was permitted to keep sculptures that gentiles made for decoration (Devar Moshe vol. 2, ḤM 122; and so wrote Tiferet Le-Moshe and Mekor Mayim Ḥayim on SA 141:8); however, in practice one should be stringent, and so wrote the Ḥida in Shiyurei Berakha 141:8, and Mishpetei Uziel vol. 2, YD 18. It is permitted to draw the Temple or its vessels at their exact size; so wrote the Ritva and Meiri on Avoda Zara 43a.

Gemara, Avoda Zara 43a: "It was taught: A person may not make a house in the pattern of the Heikhal, an akhsadra in the pattern of the Ulam, a courtyard in the pattern of the Azara, a table in the pattern of the Table, a menora in the pattern of the Menora; but he may make one of five, of six or of eight [branches]. But one of seven he may not make, even of other kinds of metal" – but of a material that is not metal it is permitted, since it is unfit for the Menora. The Rishonim wrote that the permission to make a vessel that is not exactly like the Temple vessel applies when the vessel is made in a way that disqualifies it from use in the Temple (Ritva, Meiri, Ran, Nimukei Yosef and others). Accordingly, it is also forbidden to make a menora whose height is less than eighteen tefaḥim and without cups, knobs and flowers (SA 141:8), for in this manner too it is fit (Shakh 36; Gra 39; Ḥakham Tzvi 60). And some are stringent, holding that even when the vessel is unfit for the Temple, if it closely resembles the fit vessel one should be stringent (Bekhor Shor on Rosh Ha-shana 24a, based on Maharik, Shoresh 75; cited in Pitḥei Teshuva 15). In practice, it is permitted to make a metal menora when some of the branches have no receptacle for oil, and all the more so when there are electric bulbs at the tops of its branches, for it is clear that such a menora is unfit for the Temple (Rav Tzirelson in Ma'arkhei Lev, Hashmatot 3; Rav Herzog, Psakim U-khtavim 4:43; Mishpetei Uziel vol. 2, YD 18; Ḥavalim Ba-ne'imim 3:54), and it is possible that even those who are stringent about something closely resembling it would agree to this, since it involves a great change from the Menora in the Temple (Even Yekara 1:59; Yabi'a Omer 1, YD 12).
Some are stringent not to make, for Shabbat candles, a metal menora with seven branches, even though the branches are set in a circle, for perhaps the Menora would be fit in this form too, and perhaps it is considered similar to the Temple (Bekhor Shor, Rosh Ha-shana 24a, and so decided Pitḥei Teshuva 141:14; Shemirat Shabbat Ke-hilkhata 43:2, in the note). And some permit it, for it does not resemble the Temple Menora at all, and moreover its branches do not have a receptacle for oil as in the Menora, but rather a receptacle for a wax candle or a small glass cup (Responsa Rabbeinu Ḥayim Kohen YD 25; She'ilat Shalom as cited in Darkhei Teshuva 141:56; Yabi'a Omer 1, YD 12).

sections.title_en: The Prohibition of Planting a Tree Near the Altar
sections.body_en:
The Torah forbade planting a tree near the Altar, that is, anywhere in the Azara adjacent to the Sanctuary, as it is stated (Devarim 16:21): "You shall not plant for yourself an ashera, any tree, beside the altar of the Lord your God which you shall make for yourself." Every tree is included in the prohibition, whether a fruit tree or a non-fruit-bearing tree. And even if the intention of planting it is for beauty, to glorify the Temple, the Torah forbade it, and one who transgresses and plants it is liable to lashes.

As to the reason for the mitzva, it has been explained that the Torah's intention is to distance Israel from any trace of idolatry, and therefore it forbade acting according to the customs of the idolaters, who used to plant a tree next to their altars, so that passers-by in the area would see the tree from afar and know that there was an altar there, until the identifying sign of idolatry was an altar with a tree beside it (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 6:9; Ramban, Devarim 16:21). In addition, many used to worship the tree beside the altar, to the point that those who offered sacrifices on the altar appeared to be offering to the ashera (Rashbam and Bekhor Shor, there).

One may further explain that planting a tree is a personal expression of man, who was created in the image of God and draws the word of God down to the earth through life and growth, whereas the Altar expresses withdrawal from earthly life in order to draw close, with self-sacrifice, to the supernal holiness. Therefore the place of the Altar is in the holiest place, which one can approach only after withdrawing from ordinary life, whereas the place for planting trees is throughout all the expanses of the earth, in order to draw down God's blessing to all areas of life. Accordingly, it is forbidden to plant a tree in the place of the Altar, so as not to mix the holiness that spreads through the earth with the holiness that is above the earth, and so that a person not mix his personal inclinations into the supernal holiness, in the manner of idolaters, all of whose worship is for their own benefit and who do not aim at tikkun olam (repairing the world) under the kingdom of Shaddai.

The Sages further forbade building wooden structures in the Azara, such as an akhsadra, that is, a wooden roof (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 6:10; Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 1:9). But it is permitted to bring into the Azara for a few hours a wooden structure that is not permanent, such as the platform on which the king stood when he read from the Torah at the Hakhel assembly (Yerushalmi Megilla 1:4).15

Some are stringent and forbid planting trees in the courtyard of a synagogue, for the laws of the synagogue are learned from the Temple, and in a synagogue too one should keep away from the custom of idolaters, who planted trees at their place of worship. However, a wooden structure such as an akhsadra, which is forbidden in the Temple by rabbinic decree, may be built next to the synagogue (Rabbi David Arama). And one authority added a reason for the prohibition: lest men and women sit together intermingled in the shade of the trees; and in his opinion, if trees were mistakenly planted in the courtyard of the synagogue, they must be uprooted (Maharam Schick OḤ 78-79). However, the custom of Israel is not to refrain from planting trees near a synagogue, and this is the view of most poskim (Maharsham, Rav Kook). And the Netziv wrote (Meshiv Davar 2:14) that we must not invent prohibitions of our own that are not found in the Talmud.16

notes_en.en:
According to Rashi (Devarim 16:21), the prohibition of planting a tree applies to the entire Temple Mount, and so it is explained in the view of the Tanna Kamma in the Sifrei, and so wrote the Gra (Aderet Eliyahu, Devarim 16:21). By contrast, according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 6:9) and the Ra'avad (on Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 1:9), the prohibition applies in the sanctified Azara but not on the Temple Mount and in the Ezrat Nashim, in accordance with the view of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov in the Sifrei (Kesef Mishneh, and the Mabit in Kiryat Sefer, Beit Ha-beḥira, there). And some hold that according to the Rambam too the Torah prohibition applies to the whole Temple Mount, but one receives lashes only in the Azara (Rabbi Ḥayim Ya'akov of Safed in Tzror Ha-ḥayim).
The Sages further learned (Sanhedrin 7b) from the juxtaposition of the passage on judges to the prohibition of planting a tree near the Altar, "that whoever appoints a judge who is not fit – it is as if he plants an ashera in Israel… and in a place where there are Torah scholars – it is as if he planted it beside the Altar." As it is stated (Devarim 16:18-21): "Judges and officers you shall appoint for yourself in all your gates which the Lord your God gives you, according to your tribes, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgement. You shall not pervert judgement… You shall not plant for yourself an ashera, any tree, beside the altar of the Lord your God which you shall make for yourself." The meaning of the comparison is that one who appoints an unfit judge behaves like idolaters, who prefer their own benefit to justice. And if there are Torah scholars there, it is as if he planted an ashera beside the Altar; that is, although he knows that it is easy to choose judges who are Torah scholars and to walk in the ways of God, he prefers his own benefit (see Maharal, Gur Aryeh, and Meshekh Ḥokhma there). Already at the time of planting the ashera one transgresses the prohibition, and likewise already in appointing an unfit judge one transgresses the prohibition, even though he has not yet perverted judgement (Arukh La-ner, Sanhedrin there).

Those who forbid: Rabbi David Arama on the Rambam, cited by Rabbi Akiva Eiger OḤ 150:1; Rabbi David Pardo, Tosefta Sifrei De-vei Rav, Shoftim 146. Those who permit: Maharsham 1:127; Oraḥ Mishpat 37; Heikhal Yitzḥak OḤ 10. And so it emerges from Binyan Tziyon 1:9, and from many others who dealt with related laws and did not raise this concern at all.

sections.title_en: The Prohibition of Making a Matzeva
sections.body_en:
The Torah forbade erecting a matzeva (a cultic pillar), as it is stated (Devarim 16:22): "Neither shall you set up for yourself a matzeva, which the Lord your God hates," and it is likewise stated (Vayikra 26:1): "You shall make for yourselves no idols, and a graven image or a matzeva you shall not set up for yourselves." A matzeva is a single stone, and some say also a structure of stones, which idolaters used to erect in honour of the idols, and on which they would pour libations of wine or pour oil. Likewise, some erected a matzeva next to an altar intended for sacrifices, and around the matzeva they would gather to hear the words of the priests, or they placed sculptures on it. Since it was the way of the idolaters to erect a matzeva, the Torah forbade erecting a matzeva even for the honour of Heaven (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 6:6; Sefer Ha-mitzvot, Lo Ta'aseh 11; Ramban, Devarim 16:22).

It is true that in the days of the Patriarchs a matzeva erected in honour of God was desirable, as our forefather Ya'akov did after the dream of the ladder and the divine revelation, as it is stated (Bereshit 28:18): "And he took the stone that he had put under his head, and set it up as a matzeva, and poured oil upon its top." That is to say, he set up a matzeva in remembrance of the divine revelation, to mark that this holy place is "the house of God" and "the gate of heaven." However, following the custom of the idolaters to make a matzeva for the idols, the matzeva became hateful, and we were commanded not to erect one even for the sake of God (Sifrei; Rashi and Ramban, Devarim 16:22).

Apparently, at first, when the name of God was not yet known in the world, every additional remembrance of the name of God was desirable. However, after God revealed Himself to His people Israel, commanded them to build the Temple and established precise orders for offering sacrifices on the Altar, Israel must connect to God by the paved path of the Torah, which is designed to elevate them to cleave to truth and goodness. But if a person sets up a matzeva on his own personal initiative, he will deviate from faith in God's unity and from the guidance of the Torah, becoming like the idolaters, who out of the inclination of their hearts invent modes of worship in order to entice the idols to help them fulfil their desires.

The prohibition is to make a matzeva for the sake of God's holiness or – to make the distinction – for idolatrous worship, but there is no prohibition against making a matzeva for other purposes. Accordingly, it is permitted to make a matzeva (gravestone) on a grave and write on it the name of the deceased and his virtues, so that he will be remembered. It is likewise permitted to make memorial monuments for fallen soldiers or for various events.17

notes_en.en: The need to erect memorial monuments arose after the First World War, when soldiers fell and were buried far from their homes, and the members of their communities wished to commemorate them in the cemetery of their town. After the Holocaust this need grew greater, and over the years the State of Israel became the place where the custom of erecting monuments in memory of the fallen is most widespread. At first some argued that one should not erect monuments in memory of Jews who were killed, because of the prohibition of erecting a matzeva, since we learned that it is forbidden to erect one even for the service of God. However, in practice the rabbis ruled that there is no prohibition in this, because the prohibition is to set up a matzeva connected to religious worship, whereas monuments are not intended for religious matters, and the fact that prayers are sometimes recited there is incidental, and it was not for this that the monument was erected. So responded Rav Tzirelson in Responsa Ma'arkhei Lev YD 42, regarding erecting a monument in Karlsburg in Transylvania in memory of those killed in the First World War. And so ruled Rav Uziel (Mishpetei Uziel vol. 2, YD 22) and Rav Herzog (Kol Torah 1:1) after the Holocaust. However, since at the time they were asked about this the custom was new, not practised in previous generations, they wrote that it is preferable to commemorate the fallen in the way of Yisrael Saba (the traditional way of our forefathers), by building a synagogue or a Talmud Torah. Responsa of Rav Avraham Fingerhut 18 and Minḥat Yitzḥak 1:29 also wrote that there is no prohibition in this.

sections.title_en: The Prohibition of Bowing on an Even Maskit
sections.body_en:
The Torah forbade bowing down on an even maskit (a figured or paving stone), even when the one who bows intends it for the sake of Heaven, as it is stated (Vayikra 26:1): "You shall make for yourselves no idols, and a graven image or a matzeva you shall not set up for yourselves, nor shall you place any even maskit in your land to bow down upon it, for I am the Lord your God." This prohibition, whose punishment is lashes, applies throughout the Land and the world, but in the Temple it is permitted (Megilla 22b).

Even maskit is an expression of covering, as it is stated (Shemot 33:22): "and I will cover (ve-sakoti) you with My hand" (Rashi). That is, a hewn stone that was laid on the ground and covers it. Maskit is also an expression of ornament, sekhiyat ḥemda (a delightful object), as was the custom of idolaters, who would make drawings and engravings on the stone and bow down on it. However, even if there was no ornament on the stone, it is forbidden by Torah law to bow down on it (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 6:6; Ḥinukh, mitzva 349).

This prohibition branches out from the prohibition of idolatry, for this was the practice of idolaters, who imagined that stones possess powers, and would set down a stone and bow on it in order to connect to it and receive its help. Only in the Temple, the place of faith, is there no prohibition against bowing on an even maskit, since it is clear that one is bowing to God.

A further reason for the prohibition: in the Temple there is a mitzva to pave the Azara with hewn stones, and on them people would bow to God, and it is not fitting to make other places equal to it and bow in them as one bows in the Temple (Rashi, Megilla 22b).

The Torah prohibition is to bow on a large stone that was hewn while still attached to the ground, or on a floor made of stones that were taken from their place and laid on the ground. But it is permitted to bow on a natural rock, and it is likewise permitted to bow on a brick, since it was formed artificially by mixing materials.

The Torah prohibition applies when two conditions are fulfilled in the bowing: a) on stone; b) bowing with arms and legs outstretched, that is, when one's whole body is spread out flat on the stone, and not a bow in which only one's head touches the stone (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 6:6). The Sages decreed that it is forbidden to bow even when one of the conditions is fulfilled. Accordingly: a) It is forbidden to bow on stone even without outstretched arms and legs, provided that one's head touches the stone. But if one did so not on stone, or placed something to separate between his head and the stone, or did so leaning to the right or the left, it is permitted. b) It is forbidden to bow with arms and legs outstretched on anything attached to the ground even though it is not stone; but if a cloth or a non-fixed carpet is placed on it, one will be able to bow on it with arms and legs outstretched.18

notes_en.en:
What is explained above follows the stringent view, as many of the Aḥaronim wrote. However, some hold that there is no rabbinic decree at all in this matter, and the prohibition is only what the Torah forbade, bowing with arms and legs outstretched on stone. However, an important person must turn his face aside, so that there will be no ḥillul Hashem (desecration of God's name) should he not be answered after falling on his face (Ra'avan, Or Zaru'a, and Pri Ḥadash OḤ 131:8). But as stated, many hold that by rabbinic law it is forbidden to bow on stone even without outstretched arms and legs, whenever one's head touches the stone, and only if there is something separating, or when leaning, is it permitted (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 6:7; Semag, Semak, Mordekhai, Rema 131:8, Levush 7, Olat Tamid 29, Magen Avraham 22, Pri Megadim, MB 40, Kaf Ha-ḥayim 111).
Regarding bowing with arms and legs outstretched not on stone, the poskim disagree: some say there is no prohibition at all in this (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 6:7; Or Zaru'a; Arukh Ha-shulḥan OḤ 131:18). On the other hand, some hold that even not on stone it is forbidden to bow without leaning (Rivash 412, in the name of Rav Sherira Gaon and Rabbi Yitzḥak ibn Ghiyat; Rema 131:8), and the Aḥaronim were in doubt (Magen Avraham 131:22; Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 44) whether the prohibition applies only to what is attached to the ground, but on a separating cloth it is permitted, or whether even on a separating cloth it is forbidden without leaning. And the Taz 15 was lenient.
Seemingly, since the doubt in these laws is rabbinic, one could be lenient in accordance with the Ra'avan and those who agree with him, that it is forbidden to bow only with arms and legs outstretched on stone, or at least in accordance with the Rambam and Arukh Ha-shulḥan, that there is no prohibition against bowing with arms and legs outstretched not on stone. However, the tendency of the Aḥaronim in these laws is toward stringency, that the rabbinic prohibition applies even when one condition is fulfilled: stone, or bowing with arms and legs outstretched (Rema 131:8, Levush 7, Taz 14, Magen Avraham 22, Pri Megadim, Olat Tamid 27, MB 40, Kaf Ha-ḥayim 114). But regarding the last doubt cited in the Magen Avraham, about which the Taz was lenient, one should certainly be lenient, that one may bow with arms and legs outstretched on a non-fixed carpet, as I wrote above.
The Minḥat Ḥinukh (349:1) was in doubt whether it is permitted to bow on an even maskit in the sanctified area of the Temple Mount. However, as rabbis of our generation have explained, the words of the Sages imply that people would bow on the Temple Mount even though it was paved with stone, and consequently it is understood that the mitzva to bow in the Temple applies to the entire area of the Temple Mount and not only to the area of the Azarot (El Har Ha-mor, Beirurei Halakha 6; Likrat Mikdash, siman 18; Har Ha-bayit Ke-hilkhato vol. 2, 2). Accordingly, it is permitted to bow with arms and legs outstretched on a stone floor at any place in the Temple Mount plaza that is clearly included in the sanctified part, five hundred by five hundred amot. However, regarding most places in the Temple Mount plaza there is a doubt whether they are included in the sanctified area of the Temple Mount, and in them one should be stringent regarding what is forbidden by Torah law. That is to say, it is forbidden there to bow with arms and legs outstretched on stone, but it is permitted to kneel on one's knees and press one's head to the ground on a stone floor, or to bow with arms and legs outstretched on ground that is not stone. And in these ways one may be lenient throughout the Temple Mount compound, even in a place that is apparently not part of the sanctified area, combining the view of the Ra'avan and those who agree with him. For by the letter of the law one could rule in accordance with them everywhere, since the dispute concerns a rabbinic matter, but since there is no need for it, the poskim ruled to be stringent, and perhaps they also wished to keep away from the custom of the gentiles (see Ha-maspik Le-ovdei Hashem, chapter 25; Iyunim U-meḥkarim by Rav Shaul Ḥana Kook, p. 363). But when one is around the place where there is a mitzva to bow, one may rely on the lenient opinions.
